title: Androcles and the Lion
text:
The Roman writer Aulus Gellius retold this story from the scholar Apion, who claimed to have seen its ending in Rome. A slave named Androcles ran away from a cruel master, a Roman official in Africa. He hid in a desert cave, and soon a lion limped in, groaning, and held out a swollen paw. Androcles found a large thorn buried in it, pulled it out, pressed out the pus and bound the wound.

For three years man and lion shared the cave, and the lion brought him the best parts of its kills. At last Androcles grew tired of that wild life and left. He was captured by soldiers, sent back to Rome and condemned to be thrown to the beasts in the Circus Maximus.

On the day of the games a huge lion was released against him. It ran at him, then stopped short, approached slowly, and began to wag its tail and lick his hands and feet. The crowd was astonished. When the emperor asked for an explanation, Androcles told his story, and it spread through the stands on written tablets. The people demanded that he be freed and given the lion. Afterward, Apion says, Androcles led the lion through the city on a light leash, and people gave him money and threw flowers on the lion.
lesson: Help given freely, even to a creature that cannot thank you in words, can come back when you least expect it. Gratitude is a strong bond.
date: 2nd century AD (set in the 1st century AD)
source: Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 5.14, after Apion
caveat: Apion claimed to be an eyewitness, but the tale is generally treated as a legend rather than a historical event.
